articleTitle: Project management techniques and the relevance of tools
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Project Management Tools (Digest No: 1992/046)
abstract: Summary form only given. Project management can be split into three aspects; people, techniques, and tools. The people, i.e. the project manager and the project organisation need to understand the techniques, namely a vie work breakdown structures, BCWP/ACWP, etc. in order to control the project. The tools assist in the process of control but are superfluous without an understanding of the techniques. In turn the techniques are meaningless if the people do not know how to use them. To appreciate the techniques it is important to understand the fundamentals, such as; what is a project? what is project management? and what is a project manager? With a clear understanding of these simple facts it puts into perspective the importance of techniques in respect to the control of a project. The only way to control a project is to fully understand the techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

abstract: The technical issues of which project management tool (if any) to use are insignificant compared with the business issues and how to manage people, projects and priorities; what style of projects to run; and how mature is the organisation (is every project really different from all the others). The author discusses the different needs of project managers, department managers, team leaders and team members and the key project management issues they face.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: People and project management-making it happen
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on Project Management Tools (Digest No: 1992/046)
abstract: Corporate organisations are undergoing transition to flexible and response networks embracing both customers and suppliers. But the desire for change is not always matched by an awareness of how to bring it about. The author draws upon the latest batch of an ongoing series of surveys of larger organisations. They highlight the need for clear vision and sustained top management commitment. Transformation is taking longer to achieve than was first thought. In a growing number of organisations there is disillusion, and a gulf between expectation and achievement. In particular, many managers are not being equipped with the project management and other skills to bring about corporate transformation. The author identifies the skills that are sought and suggests that new attitudes and approaches are needed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
